<reason>On the motion as written, A kept the stronger surviving path. The conjunctive text covers social-insurance eligibility, and B never adequately answered that branch: B4 conceded contributory schemes rightly cover such workers for pensions/sickness, leaving only the "decoration" line, which collapses against the uncontested status quo where platform earnings count for nothing. A also answered both pressure questions with a concrete financing design (flat pro-rata levy, partial-earnings offsets) and a favorable comparison: imperfect coverage versus total invisibility. B argued more crisply — landing the "fix both problems" versus thermometer contradiction, the "starve don't deactivate" mechanism, the waitress-analogy collapse, and the taxpayer-cost reversal — and had cleaner execution, while A was clipped twice and left the reclassification-foreclosure point unanswered. But B's net-harm route arrived late and speculative, leaves genuinely flexible workers uncovered, and B's own reclassification remedy was shown to run on the very earnings records the motion mandates. B won rebuttal craft; A won the decision-relevant substance.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's exposure of A's internal contradiction: records sold in the opening as "the fix for both problems at once" (A1.5), then defended in rebuttal as never meant to touch separations (A2.4) — "the motion mandates the thermometer and calls it the cure" — compounded by the point that platforms facing liability will stop deactivating and start starving workers, leaving an earnings feed blind to the one event UI exists to adjudicate. The most damaging exchange of the debate, though not enough to defeat the motion's full conjunctive scope.</best_rebuttal>
